confidence_rationale: This is the canonical review establishing that the cerebellum computes a forward-model prediction error on the sensory CONSEQUENCES of motor commands (an efference-copy-based motor-sensory error), and that this error signal is computationally and anatomically distinct from generic sensory prediction (which does not require an efference copy / motor-command input at all). That distinction maps closely onto MECH-069's E1 (sensory prediction error, no action-conditioning) vs. E2 (motor-sensory error on z_gamma, requires knowing what action was taken) split. As a 1998 theoretical review rather than a fresh empirical measurement, it is foundational-canonical evidence for the computational ARGUMENT that these two error types are structurally different, but it predates and does not itself measure REE's specific E1/E2/E3 architecture, and it says nothing about a harm/goal channel (E3).
failure_signatures: This is a review/theoretical synthesis, not a fresh measurement -- it establishes the computational architecture argument (forward models require efference copy, hence a motor-conditioned error type) rather than new data discriminating E1 from E2 in REE's specific latent-space sense (z_gamma).

The paper explicitly notes cerebellar climbing fibers also carry information about errors in the PREDICTION of aversive events, not only motor performance errors -- which complicates a clean E2-is-purely-motor / E3-is-purely-harm partition and should be read alongside the Schultz 1998 counterweight entry in this same directory.

mapping.source_claim_statement: The cerebellum implements forward internal models that predict the sensory consequences of motor commands using an efference copy of the command itself; this motor-conditioned prediction error is generated by mechanisms (climbing fiber teaching signals onto Purkinje cells) that are anatomically and computationally separate from generic sensory prediction, which requires no motor/efference-copy input.
mapping.ree_translation: MECH-069 splits E1 (sensory prediction error, no action-conditioning, indexes world-model fidelity) from E2 (motor-sensory error on z_gamma, requires the action taken, indexes motor-model fidelity). Wolpert, Miall & Kawato provide the canonical neuroscientific grounding for exactly this distinction: a forward model that predicts the sensory outcome of a specific efferent command is a structurally different computation from passive sensory prediction, and the brain implements it with a dedicated circuit (cerebellar climbing-fiber teaching signal) rather than folding it into generic sensory prediction.
mapping.mapping_caveat: This is a review synthesizing motor-control theory and cerebellar physiology, not a study of REE's specific z_gamma object-level representation, and it long predates REE. The efference-copy argument transfers cleanly to the E1-vs-E2 conceptual distinction, but the paper cannot speak to whether E2 as REE implements it (action-conditioned prediction over a bound multisensory object space) behaves the way cerebellar forward models do over raw motor kinematics -- that generalization is REE's own architectural choice, not something this paper tests.
mapping.source_context: Theoretical/computational neuroscience review, synthesizing human and animal cerebellar physiology and motor-control modeling literature; not a REE-specific or agent-architecture study.

confidence_components.notes: Canonical, extremely widely cited foundational review for the forward-model/efference-copy account of motor prediction error -- high source quality within its domain. Mapping fidelity and transfer risk are both moderate: it grounds the E1-vs-E2 conceptual split well but is silent on REE's object-level z_gamma implementation and on the E3/harm arm entirely.
